why: Survey sampled only dog owners, not all city residents — a non-representative subgroup. Answer D: sample is biased.
Random sample from people who liked the book; results generalize only to that group. Answer D: most book-likers will dislike the movie. Must resist over-generalizing to all moviegoers.
Neither statement must be true: 87% is an estimate, not the exact population value, and another sample need not yield the same result. Answer A.
Random sample from history professors at CSU; results generalize to all history professors at all California State Universities (C).
None of the three statements must be true: 78% is a sample estimate, another local sample and another city's sample need not match. Answer A.
Random selection from baobab trees of a certain age in one habitat; results apply to all trees of that age in this habitat. OCR damage obscures exact age but scope logic is clear.
Families at a playground are a convenience sample biased toward families with children, not representative of the community. Answer C.
Voluntary website poll of cable news viewers — self-selected, not a random sample of the US population. Answer B.
Random sample from one middle school; results generalize to all students at that school (B), not the whole city.
Random sample from all trivia teams in the tournament; largest population is all teams in the tournament (D). Practice-hours table is extra info not needed for scope.
Random sample of fourth-graders at one school; results generalize to all fourth-grade students at the school (B).
